rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence yet and maximal uncertainty across all design dimensions (modality, profile type, encoder, aggregation, fusion). The most informative first experiment is a simple, fast, interpretable baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000. This establishes (1) a performance floor for the pipeline, (2) the contribution of the RNA modality alone, and (3) a reference against which every subsequent experiment (adding image, switching to multiprofile, upgrading the encoder, or changing fusion) can be directly compared. Choosing the simplest encoder (PCA) also minimizes computational cost and reduces the risk of a failed run, preserving budget for more informative follow-ups. This is the best use of the first experiment because it maximally reduces uncertainty about the baseline and sets up clean ablations for all downstream design decisions.

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) has been completed, yielding accuracy 0.485 / F1 0.464. This gives us a single unimodal (RNA) baseline but zero information about the image modality's contribution. Uncertainty: The most critical open question for a multimodal study is whether the image modality is informative at all and how it compares to RNA. Without an image-only baseline, any future multimodal result would be uninterpretable—we could not distinguish whether gains come from image features, the fusion mechanism, or simply a stronger unimodal model. What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) establishes the image-only baseline using the simplest, most standard image encoder and the same singleprofile setting as config_001, isolating the modality effect. Why this is the best next experiment: It reduces the highest-impact uncertainty with a clean, minimal-configuration comparison. Once both unimodal baselines are known, subsequent experiments (multiprofile, multimodal fusion, encoder choices) can be interpreted against a well-characterized landscape, making every remaining budget slot more informative.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA-2000 and single profile (config_001) achieves 48.5% accuracy, far outperforming image-only ResNet50 (20.8%), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether aggregating multiple profiles (multiprofile) can improve on the single-profile RNA baseline. Question tested: config_002 isolates the effect of multiprofile + avgpool aggregation while keeping the same PCA-2000 encoder as the best baseline, making it a clean single-variable comparison to config_001. Why this is the best next experiment: With only 2 completed runs, the most efficient use of the next budget slot is to extend the strongest known direction (RNA) with the simplest new design axis (profile aggregation). If multiprofile+avgpool improves accuracy, it confirms aggregation is valuable and motivates testing transformer aggregation (config_003) next; if it does not, it tells us the single profile already captures the relevant signal and we should pivot to encoder improvements (scvi/scgpt). This experiment reduces the most critical uncertainty—whether profile aggregation matters—while building directly on the best evidence.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a large improvement over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming multiprofile aggregation is highly beneficial. However, we have no data on whether transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool for multiprofile RNA. Uncertainty: whether the more expressive transformer aggregation captures inter-profile dependencies that simple averaging misses, or whether avgpool already captures most of the signal. This experiment (config_003) is a clean A/B test against config_002, changing only the aggregation method (avgpool → transformer) while holding encoder, profile setting, and modality fixed. The result directly determines which aggregation strategy to carry forward into all subsequent experiments (better encoders, multimodal fusion), making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with pca_n2000/multiprofile/avgpool (config_002) achieves 0.591 acc, the best result so far, while image-only with resnet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208. We have no multimodal result yet. Question: Does combining image features with the strong RNA signal via simple concat fusion improve upon the RNA-only baseline? This directly tests whether the image modality contributes useful complementary information or merely adds noise. Why this is the best next experiment: The multimodal-vs-unimodal question has the highest information value under budget constraints—if concat fusion with the best-known RNA setup fails to beat 0.591, it strongly suggests image features (at least from resnet50) are not contributing, allowing us to deprioritize the ~36 multimodal configs and focus remaining budget on RNA encoder selection (scvi, scgpt). If it does help, it confirms fusion is worth exploring and motivates testing weighted fusion and ViT-L image encoder next. Using avgpool (proven best aggregation) and pca_n2000 (proven best encoder so far) isolates the fusion question with minimal confounding.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result so far at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, confirming that multiprofile + avgpool + multimodal concat is a strong backbone. However, the fusion strategy (concat vs weighted) is completely untested. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation, or is the benefit of adding the image modality independent of how the two representations are combined? This is a clean single-variable A/B against config_018 (only fusion changes from concat to weighted), so any difference is directly attributable to the fusion choice. Rationale: Under a limited budget, testing the fusion mechanism on the already-validated backbone is the lowest-uncertainty, highest-information next step. If weighted fusion improves performance, it tells us the modalities contribute unequally and we should explore weighting further; if it is comparable, we can rule out fusion as a critical design axis and redirect effort to untested encoders (scvi/scgpt, ViT-L) where larger gains are likely.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.639 acc / 0.620 F1. Adding image (resnet50) to the validated RNA pipeline (config_002, 0.591) yielded a meaningful ~5-point gain, confirming the image modality contributes. However, the image encoder dimension is entirely unexplored beyond resnet50. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a substantially larger, higher-capacity pretrained ViT) further improve multimodal performance, or is resnet50 already near the ceiling for the image contribution? Why this is the best next experiment: config_025 changes only the image encoder while holding every other parameter at its empirically validated best setting (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion, pca_n2000). This isolates the image-encoder effect cleanly. If it improves, it identifies a clear exploitation path; if it does not, it confirms resnet50 is sufficient and redirects attention to the RNA encoder dimension. This is a high-information, low-risk extension of the current best configuration under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality (0.591 RNA-only vs 0.208 image-only), and the current best configuration (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder. We have zero data on alternative RNA encoders (scvi_n200, scgpt), making this the largest unexplored design axis. Question: Does a learned biological embedding (scvi_n200) outperform a linear PCA projection in the multimodal setting where RNA carries most of the signal? This experiment tests scvi_n200 in the exact best-known multimodal scaffold (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted), isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding all other factors at their empirically best values. Rationale: Since RNA drives most of the predictive signal, the encoder choice is a first-order design decision. A positive result would open a high-impact improvement direction; a null or negative result would efficiently rule out that axis. This is more informative than testing transformer aggregation (already strongly disfavored by the 7-point RNA-only gap) or re-testing image encoders (near-tie between resnet50 and ViT-L).

The strongest evidence so far is that switching the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 in the multimodal/multiprofile/avgpool/weighted setting (config_031 vs config_019) yielded a substantial +3.9 pp accuracy gain (0.678 vs 0.639), making the RNA encoder the most impactful design axis. However, we have only tested one learned encoder (scvi_n200) and cannot yet tell whether this gain is specific to scvi or a general property of learned RNA encoders. config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is a clean A/B comparison against config_031 on the single variable of RNA encoder. It will clarify whether scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, or whether scvi_n200 is uniquely suited to this task. Under a limited budget, resolving the most influential design decision (RNA encoder choice) before further exploring the image-encoder or aggregation dimensions is the highest-information next step: if scgpt is competitive, it opens an additional viable path; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and can commit remaining budget to refining the image-encoder and fusion choices around it.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.678 vs 0.639 for pca_n2000, 0.525 for scgpt), and weighted fusion with avgpool aggregation is the strongest multimodal recipe (config_031: 0.678). The image encoder choice (resnet50 vs imagenet_vit_l) showed a negligible gap with pca_n2000 (0.639 vs 0.635), but that comparison was made with a weaker RNA encoder. With scvi_n200's richer latent representation, the image branch's contribution may shift, and a larger pretrained ViT could provide complementary spatial features that a CNN misses. This experiment tests whether swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l in the current best configuration yields further gains, directly exploiting the strongest evidence (scvi_n200 + weighted + avgpool) while resolving the remaining uncertainty about the optimal image encoder in this regime. It is the lowest-risk, highest-information next step: if it improves, we identify the full best config; if not, we confirm resnet50 suffices and can pivot to other axes (e.g., transformer aggregation or concat fusion) with confidence.
